summary: For children aged 5–7 learning to perform simple fair tests: turn a real question into a doing-and-observing loop — change ONE thing, keep the rest the same, watch and describe what happens, then use that observed result to answer the starting question. Because the objective is to PERFORM a test, the enacted test the child runs (on-screen or with real ramps/materials) is the core; tap-to-reveal scenes, planning talk, and a short review act as primers or checks around the actual doing.
misconceptions: Thinking a test is just playing or 'having a go', not a way to answer a question.
Changing several things at once, so it's unclear what caused the result.
Deciding the answer from what you already believed rather than from what you observed.
Believing the 'right' result is the one that matches your prediction.
Not connecting the result back to the original question (doing the test but not drawing the answer).
Thinking you only need to do a test once and can't repeat or check it.

activities.title: Test Bench: which ramp sends the car furthest?
steps: Start from a real question the child cares about, e.g. 'Which ramp makes the toy car roll the FURTHEST?'
Say your guess first (predict), then set the ramp low, release the car, and mark where it stops with a flag.
Change ONE thing — raise the ramp height — release the same car again, and mark where it stops with a new flag.
Compare the flags and finish the sentence 'The car goes furthest when the ramp is…' by choosing the answer the flags actually show.
If tempted to also swap the car or the floor surface at the same time, change only one thing so you can tell what made the difference.
activities.insight: A test is a way to make the world answer your question: when I change one thing and watch, the result shows me the answer instead of me just guessing.

activities.title: Which surface lets the car roll furthest? (real materials)
steps: Set out a ramp, a toy car and three floor surfaces at the bottom of the ramp — carpet, smooth wood, bubble wrap — with the question 'which surface lets the car roll the furthest?'
Release (don't push) the same car from the same spot on the same ramp onto each surface in turn, changing only the surface.
Watch and describe how far the car goes each time (mark or tally the distance).
Keep everything else the same each time so each surface gets a fair go.
Finish by answering the question directly from your own marks, e.g. 'the [surface], because the car rolled furthest on it' (add 'every time' only if you repeated the runs and it won each time).
activities.insight: To compare fairly, release the same car from the same start point the same way (no extra push) and change only the surface — then the answer comes from what you observed, not what you expected.

activities.title: Spot the test: a primer before you build one
steps: Explore a test set-up by revealing its parts, e.g. tap the ramp to see how high it is, tap the car to see how far it went.
Name what the test is trying to find out (its question) and what single thing is being changed.
Then move on to running your own test, where YOU change the one thing and generate the result.
activities.insight: A test has a question, one thing that changes, and a result you watch — and a real test means you change it yourself and see what happens.

activities.title: Plan-a-test talk with a science friend
steps: Before testing, talk through a plan: 'What one thing will you change? What will you keep the same? What will you watch?'
Run the real or on-screen test, then talk about the result: 'What did you see? So what is your answer?'
activities.insight: Planning out loud helps you pick the one thing to change and decide what to watch, so your result can actually answer the question.

activities.title: Check the loop (quick review)
steps: Answer a few pictorial checks: 'What should you change to test this?'
Put the steps in order: question → test → observe → answer.
Read an answer off a described result: given what happened, say which thing won.
activities.insight: A good test changes one thing, watches the result, and uses that result to answer the question.

checkQuestion: Here are three ramp surfaces — carpet, smooth wood, and bubble wrap — a toy car, and a ramp. We want to find out which surface lets the car roll the furthest. Set it up and try it, then tell me which surface won and how you know. I'll watch while you do it.
checkAnswer: The child releases the same car from the same place on the same ramp onto each surface in turn (changing only the surface), watches and describes how far the car goes each time, and answers the question from what they saw — for example, 'the smooth wood, because the car rolled furthest on it every time.'
